summary: Initial discovery to understand Opaline's p95 streaming latency SLO, concurrency targets, and hosting constraints. Customer leaning toward hosted for time-to-market but has compliance questions that may push to Dedicated or Private. Agreed to run a short benchmark and exchange save sample prompts and infra details.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Dr. Nora Ruiz (CTO): Nora here.
[00:08] Samir (Head of ML): Samir on.
[00:10] Jo Park (Infra): Jo here.
[00:12] Liam (SE): Liam from Redwood.
[00:15] Ava (Product): Ava joining.
[00:18] Maya: Great. Our goal today is to understand your streaming SLOs, concurrency, token/sec expectations, and any security or hosting constraints — Hosted, Dedicated, or Private. Samir, do you want to give a quick rundown of the use case?
[00:30] Samir: Sure. We're building a real-time clinical summarization assistant for triage nurses. The UX expects partial token streaming — so token-per-second looks and p95 latency matter a lot. We're aiming for p95 latency under 400ms for the short responses (50-150 tokens), and for longer summaries (500-1k tokens) we care about throughput — something like sustained 600-1,200 tokens/sec per inference path.
[00:58] Maya: Okay, so two buckets: low-latency short responses and high-throughput long summaries. Helpful. Do you have concurrency targets?
[01:06] Dr. Nora: Peak is around 180 concurrent sessions during shift changes, sustained around 60–80. We might burst to 250 for events.
[01:20] Jo: And one note — our hospital network requires data residency in us-east and strict audit logging. We also need SSO/SAML and KMS integration.
[01:30] Liam: Makes sense. From a hosting perspective, Hosted Redwood API can usually hit low latency with our optimized runtime and prefix caching, but for strict residency and KMS/HSM you might look at Dedicated or Private. There's always a tradeoff — Dedicated gives you reserved pools (predictable throughput) and VPC endpoints, Private is customer-managed and can sit inside your VPC.
[01:52] Speaker 5: Quick question, how does KV cache come into play for streaming?
[01:56] Liam: Good Q. KV cache (we sometimes say V K cache in logs) helps for repeated context; for streaming it's less about prefix reuse and more about avoiding cold starts for the same model and quantization path. For long summaries we rely on continuous batching and pipeline parallelism to hit higher tokens/sec.
[02:18] Samir: What's realistic tokens/sec per GPU for your common LLMs? We plan to use a 7B->13B family open model for inference.
[02:27] Liam: For a 13B quantized variant on A100s or similar, we typically see 800–1,500 tokens/sec at steady state depending on sequence length and micro-batching. On T4/low-memory instances it's lower. If you need the 1,200 tokens/sec target per inference path, Dedicated with autoscaled pools is safest.
[02:45] Maya: Can I add: p95 for streaming is often dominated by network + first token emission; we instrument token latency and server-side queueing. For short 50–150 token responses, hitting p95 < 400ms is doable on Hosted in most regions; but if you need strict SLA at peak concurrency we recommend Dedicated.
[03:04] Dr. Nora: We also need to consider fallback if a model is preempted or cold started — we can't have triage stalls. What's your graceful degradation story?
[03:12] Liam: We have routing policies and automatic fallback to smaller quantized model variants, plus regional fallback. For Dedicated you can pin model versions, reserve burst capacity, and set automatic fallback rules. Hosted has automatic fallbacks too but less deterministic behavior under very high burst.
[03:28] Ava: And regarding quality — how do we avoid quantization regressions for clinical language?
[03:33] Liam: Redwood Optimize offers model/quantization recommendations and quality monitors tied to your evaluation prompts. We can run evals before and after quantization. For clinical use we'd recommend a pilot to sanity-check output quality on your gold prompt set.
[03:49] Jo: On the compliance side — SOC2 Type II, SSO, RBAC, and KMS are non-negotiable. Can Hosted meet that?
[03:58] Maya: Hosted is SOC2, supports SAML SSO and RBAC for the control plane. For customer-controlled KMS/HSM and strict VPC-only access, Dedicated or Private is the path. We can share our security pack.
[04:10] Samir: For benchmarking, what's the recommended sample set? We can supply anonymized triage transcripts and a set of long summaries. We want to measure p95 token emission, overall tokens/sec, and concurrency scaling.
[04:22] Liam: Perfect. If you can supply 200 short prompt samples and 50 long-summary samples we can run both streaming and non-streaming runs. We'll produce p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec curves and a cost estimate.
[04:35] Dr. Nora: Timeline — we want results before leadership review 2025-09-10. Is that feasible?
[04:40] Maya: Yes, if you send samples and the infra doc by 2025-09-02 we'll aim to deliver by 2025-09-08.
[04:47] Speaker 5: Will you set up a canary or pilot in our environment?
[04:50] Liam: For Dedicated or Private, we can set up a small reserved pilot cluster inside your VPC — we do pilot installs with limited capacity for a couple of weeks. Hosted pilot can be done faster but won't have the same network isolation.
[05:02] Jo: What's the expected latency delta between Hosted and Dedicated in practice?
[05:06] Liam: If Hosted is in the same region and you don't need VPC egress, the raw server-side latency is similar. Dedicated can reduce tail variance because you don't get noisy-neighbor interference and you can reserve capacity to avoid queuing. In numbers, p95 difference might be 20–60ms in many cases but can be larger under bursts.
[05:25] Samir: We care a lot about p95 tails — the triage UX shows a spinner and clinicians notice any stall. Do you recommend prewarming?
[05:34] Maya: Yes — prefix caching, warm pools, and cold-start mitigation are key. For streaming, first token emission is critical — we can prewarm top N models and keep small pools hot during shift windows.
[05:44] Dr. Nora: Okay, let's talk capacity. If we have 180 concurrent short sessions at peak with avg 80 tokens each, quick math — what's the token/sec requirement?
[05:55] Liam: Rough calc: 180 sessions * 80 tokens = 14,400 tokens total. If those are emitted over ~3 seconds (streaming), do the math: 4.8k tokens/sec. But distribution matters — not all start same time. We size for 95th percentile concurrency shape. That suggests multiple GPUs and batching layers; Dedicated makes that planner easier.
[06:18] Jo: What about autoscaling speed? We can't tolerate slow spin-up when a burst hits during a code 10.
[06:23] Liam: Our autoscaler can spin up cache-warmed instances with a warm-up pattern, but there's always a small lead time for allocating new GPUs. That's why burst capacity and reserved headroom are recommended for critical peaks.
[06:36] Speaker 5: Any thoughts on quantization tradeoffs for medical text?
[06:40] Liam: Aggressive quantization (4-bit) can hurt subtle language patterns; we'd recommend 8-bit or mixed-quant with eval checks. Redwood Optimize can suggest the best profile per model and per prompt set.
[06:51] Samir: For the benchmark, can you produce per-token cost estimates and an ops guide so we can justify Dedicated?
[06:58] Maya: Yes — we'll include a cost model: tokens/sec vs cost/hour and predicted monthly spend under your traffic shapes.
[07:06] Jo: Network isolation specifics — for Dedicated we get a VPC endpoint? How do we manage KMS keys?
[07:12] Liam: Dedicated supports private connectivity (VPC peering/PrivateLink depending on cloud). Customers can bring their own KMS keys for encrypting stored artifacts and some secrets. For full HSM integration you'd look at Private or on-prem packaging.
[07:26] Dr. Nora: Any regulatory audits required for our customers? We may need evidence of encryption at rest and detailed audit logs for a HIPAA review.
[07:34] Maya: We provide audit logs and can map logging controls; for HIPAA-level evidence we typically recommend Dedicated or Private to ensure contractual terms and covered controls. We'll hand over SOC2 docs and a HIPAA appendix where appropriate.
[07:46] Samir: Back to the numbers — can you run a quick back-of-envelope showing GPU counts for our steady and peak?
[07:52] Liam: Sure; for steady 60–80 concurrency targeting ~1k tokens/sec per long inference path we might need 2–3 GPUs depending on model. Peak 180–250 with bursts could push to 6–8 GPUs if you want headroom. We'll provide a sizing spreadsheet.
[08:08] Ava: On the integration side, we plan to call your streaming API via our Node service. Any special SDK or guidance?
[08:14] Liam: We have Node and Python SDKs with streaming endpoints and examples. For clinical workloads, instrument retries, idempotency keys, and token-level tracing. We'll share an integration checklist.
[08:26] Jo: For the benchmark, do you need SSH to anything or just prompt payloads?
[08:30] Liam: Prompt payloads and a small load profile are fine for Hosted benchmarks. For Dedicated/private we may ask for network tests or a small VPN setup for pilot.
[08:40] Dr. Nora: What's the typical time to deploy Dedicated pilot?
[08:44] Maya: From contract to small pilot it's usually 2–4 weeks depending on approvals and network setup. Hosted pilot can start in days.
[08:52] Samir: Are there any gotchas with streaming that you've seen?
[08:56] Liam: Yes — client-side timeouts, middlebox buffering, and server-side queueing. Middlebox buffering can delay token delivery; we recommend HTTP/2 streaming or websockets. Also ensure your frontend doesn't aggregate tokens unintentionally.
[09:10] Maya: Also watch for prompt size and truncation; long context can increase latency substantially. Consider retrieval-augmented pieces with short prompt windows.
[09:19] Speaker 5: Any planned maintenance windows that affect p95?
[09:22] Maya: We have scheduled maintenance but for Dedicated customers we coordinate windows and for Hosted we give advance notice and can offer resilience via multi-region routing.
[09:33] Jo: For our checklist, we'll need: security pack, sample sizing spreadsheet, benchmark plan, and pilot terms.
[09:40] Maya: We'll send those after the call.
[09:43] Liam: Next step — Samir sends anonymized prompts + concurrency curve, Jo sends infra doc. We'll run benchmarks and come back with p95 and tokens/sec report.
[09:53] Dr. Nora: Sounds good. A couple of quick clarifying Qs: how do you handle audit log retention?
[09:58] Maya: Audit logs retention is configurable; we offer default retention windows and longer retention as an add-on with Dedicated/Enterprise.
[10:07] Samir: One more — how easy to switch from Hosted pilot to Dedicated?
[10:11] Liam: We try to make switching smooth — same API surface. There's a migration plan: pin model versions, test on Dedicated pilot, then cut traffic. Some stateful caches might need reseeding.
[10:22] Ava: Ok that answers our main concerns.
[10:25] Maya: Great — we'll follow up with the artifact pack and get the benchmark scheduled. Thanks everyone.
[10:30] Dr. Nora: Thanks.
[10:32] Samir: Thanks all.
[10:34] Jo: Bye.
[10:35] Maya: Bye.

Note: transcription had minor mislabels (Speaker 5) and some garbled words around KV cache (appears as V K cache in automated transcript). Benchmarks to include: streaming p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec steady-state, cost per 1M tokens, and suggested Dedicated config.
